title: Economic Outlook Publication - Building the Economics Function Retirement Did Not Have
situation: The retirement businesses were planning and forecasting with no economic input. Macro assumptions were implicit, inconsistent across regions, and never challenged. The firm had a Global Chief Economist, but her work was not reaching Retirement in any usable form.
obstacle: Nobody had asked for this and there was no mandate to build it. Economists inside large organizations are routinely ignored, cancelled from meetings, and second-guessed by people with no training. Creating a standing claim on the Chief Economist's time required making the case unprompted and then sustaining a cadence that had no owner.
actions: Approached the Global Chief Economist directly and made the case that the retirement businesses were not getting enough economic attention
Converted a single meeting into a standing quarterly session with an agreed format
Ran the session for four years, questioning the macro view on rates, inflation, GDP, markets, central bank expectations, and political risk
Added the interpretation layer translating the macro view into expected business impact across Canada, the U.S., and Asia
Directed the drafting team and held final editorial review, editing and adding content before publication
Published the outlook to leaders across the organization on a quarterly cadence
Sustained the cadence through the Chief Economist's leave, when her macro economist took over the sessions
results: Changed how the retirement businesses forecast
Anticipated contribution growth patterns through the great resignation
Directed effort toward contribution rate strengthening as inflation rose
Established why withdrawals were rising as interest rates rose
Produced targets built on defensible economic assumptions, so misses were understood rather than misattributed
Held up through COVID and the years following
fullStory: The retirement businesses were making planning decisions with no economic input. I went to the Global Chief Economist and argued that Retirement was not getting enough economic attention. Nobody asked me to do this. It started as one meeting and became a standing quarterly session I ran for four years. The format settled quickly: she gave the current view on rates, inflation, GDP, markets, central bank expectations and political risk, I questioned it and added what it meant for the businesses in Canada, the U.S., and Asia, my team drafted the report, and I did the final edit and added content before it went out to leaders across the organization. When she went on leave her macro economist took it over and the cadence held. The output was not a newsletter. It changed how we forecast. We saw the contribution growth shift through the great resignation, we put energy into contribution rate strengthening as inflation rose, and we understood why withdrawals climbed as rates rose instead of guessing. It also meant we set targets we could defend, so when we missed we knew why rather than inventing a reason after the fact.
